proof:
# Power concavity of sampled tails for root degrees one, two, and three

Let d be one of 1,2,3. Let a_l,...,a_r be strictly positive real numbers
such that h_i=a_i^(1/d) is a concave sequence. Put F_i=sum_(j=i)^r a_j.
Then

    i -> F_i^(1/(d+1)),  i=l,...,r,                    (1)

is a concave sequence. The extra value F_(r+1)=0 is excluded. Consequently,
if the probability masses a_i/sum a_i have integer mean m, each closed
tail at m has probability at least

    ((d+1)/(d+2))^(d+1)=gamma_(d+1).                  (2)

The constant in (2) is sharp as an infimum. These are scalar statements;
no assertion about oblique mixed-integer cuts is made.

## 1. Reduction to arithmetic root sequences

Write p=1/(d+1). At an interior index i set F=F_i, A=a_(i-1), B=a_i.
If A<=B, then the desired midpoint inequality follows from
F_(i-1)+F_(i+1)=2F+A-B<=2F and concavity of t^p.

If A>B, put delta=A^(1/d)-B^(1/d)>0 and q=B^(1/d)/delta. Concavity
of h and positivity of h_(i+1) give q>1 and

    a_(i+j)<=delta^d (q-j)_+^d.

Thus F<=F_max=delta^d S_d(q), where

    S_d(q)=sum_(j>=0)(q-j)_+^d.

It suffices to establish the desired midpoint inequality at F_max.
Indeed define

    H(t)=(1+At)^p+(1-Bt)^p,    0<=t<=1/B.

This is concave, with H(0)=2. Its secant slope from zero is nonincreasing.
Therefore H(1/F_max)<=2 implies H(1/F)<=2 whenever B<=F<=F_max.
Multiplication by F^p gives

    (F+A)^p+(F-B)^p<=2F^p.

The arithmetic case at F_max is exactly

    S_d(q+1)^p+S_d(q-1)^p<=2 S_d(q)^p,                (3)

since S_d(q+1)=S_d(q)+(q+1)^d and S_d(q-1)=S_d(q)-q^d.

## 2. Arithmetic roots: exact polynomial certificates

Write q=m+rho with m an integer and 0<=rho<1. Holding rho fixed, each
S_d(q) at the points q-1,q,q+1 is the value of the same polynomial in q.
Here q>1 guarantees q-1>=rho and all three values are positive (if rho=0,
then q is an integer at least 2).

Set x=q+1/2. The three power-sum identities are

 d=1:  S_1(q)=(x^2-c)/2,
       c=(rho-1/2)^2;

 d=2:  S_2(q)=(x^3-x/4-c)/3,
       c=rho^3-(3/2)rho^2+rho/2,
       |c|<=1/(12 sqrt(3));

 d=3:  S_3(q)=(x^4-x^2/2+c)/4,
       c=1/16-rho^2(1-rho)^2,   0<=c<=1/16.

These follow by subtracting consecutive ordinary power-sum polynomials;
they also hold at the first point q=rho, where the sum equals rho^d.
The bound in the d=2 line follows by differentiating its cubic on [0,1].
For each fixed rho the indicated polynomial is positive and increasing
for q>=rho>0, and for q>0 when rho=0.

For a positive polynomial P, the sign of the second derivative of
P^(1/(d+1)) is the sign of

    E=P P''-[d/(d+1)](P')^2.

Constant positive scale factors do not change this sign. Direct
calculations give:

 d=1, P=x^2-c:
    E=-2c<=0.

 d=2, P=x^3-x/4-c:
    E=-x^2/2-6cx-1/24
      =-(x+6c)^2/2+18c^2-1/24<=0.

 d=3, P=x^4-x^2/2+c:
    E=(12x^2-1)c-x^4-x^2/4
      <=(12x^2-1)/16-x^4-x^2/4
      =-(x^2-1/4)^2<=0.

For the last inequality x>=1/2, so 12x^2-1>=0. Thus, for each fixed
rho, the polynomial root is concave throughout the interval needed to
compare q-1,q,q+1. This proves (3) and hence (1).

## 3. Jensen and the exact closed-tail constant

Normalize sum a_i=1. If there is more than one support index, the mean
m lies strictly between l and r. Interpolate the sequence in (1) linearly;
Jensen at the integer mean gives

    F_m^p>=sum_i a_i F_i^p.

Since a_i=F_i-F_(i+1), the right side is the upper-endpoint Riemann sum
of the increasing function t^p on the tail-value partition of [0,1].
It is at least integral_0^1 t^p dt=(d+1)/(d+2). Raise to the power d+1.
Reflection gives the other tail. A singleton support is immediate.
The terminal zero appears only as a partition endpoint, never as a
concavity node.

## 4. Sharpness with exactly integer means

For L>1 let a_j(L)=(L-j)_+^d for nonnegative integer j. Their positive
support is finite and their root sequence is affine. The normalized mean
m(L) is continuous, including at integer L because new endpoint masses
are born with value zero. It is strictly increasing for L>1: on every
fixed support interval the likelihood ratio a_j(L)/a_i(L), for j>i,
strictly increases with L, which implies strict increase of the mean.
The standard covariance proof is immediate by expanding the difference
of the two weighted means as a sum over ordered pairs i<j. At changes
of support, the newly positive largest index reinforces this order.

As L tends to infinity, Riemann sums give

    m(L)/L -> [integral_0^1 t(1-t)^d dt]
                      /[integral_0^1 (1-t)^d dt] =1/(d+2).

Also m(L)->0 as L decreases to 1. Hence, for every positive integer k,
there exists L_k>1 with m(L_k)=k, and L_k tends to infinity. In particular
k/L_k tends to 1/(d+2). A second Riemann-sum limit gives

 sum_(j>=k) a_j(L_k)/sum_j a_j(L_k)
   -> [integral_(1/(d+2))^1 (1-t)^d dt]
                  /[integral_0^1 (1-t)^d dt]
   =((d+1)/(d+2))^(d+1).

Thus the closed-tail bound is sharp even with an exactly integer mean.

## 5. Scope and a useful caution

For one integer coordinate and continuous dimension d<=3, positive
fiber volumes have concave d-th roots by Brunn-Minkowski. Therefore
(2) applies to every vertical closed cap through an integer-base mixed
centroid. It is a strictly stronger vertical estimate than 1/e.

No statement for arbitrary d is inferred from this proof. In particular,
the fixed-fraction power-sum polynomial root need not be concave for
higher degrees, so extrapolating the polynomial argument is unjustified.
